html:
The Nez Perce, who call themselves Nimíipuu, "the people", are an Indigenous people of the Columbia Plateau, in what is now Idaho, Oregon and Washington. Their homeland has been lived in for at least 11,500 years.

They spoke a Sahaptian language and lived along the Clearwater, Snake and Salmon rivers, fishing salmon and digging camas roots. After they gained horses in the 1700s they bred large herds and became known for the spotted Appaloosa. Their trade reached from the Pacific coast to the plains of Montana. The French name, "pierced nose", fits their neighbours better than it fits them.

In 1805 they fed and helped the starving Lewis and Clark Expedition. An 1855 treaty left them a large reservation, but after gold was found a new treaty in 1863 cut it to a tenth. Bands that refused to move fought the Nez Perce War of 1877. Chief Joseph and other leaders led some 800 people over 1,000 miles toward Canada before surrendering in Montana, just short of the border.

Their neighbours on the plateau included the Cayuse, and the modern Nimiipuu reservation is in Idaho.
